analysis.one_liner: Shields gun makers, sellers, and trade associations from lawsuits over criminal misuse of their products.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Judiciary Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any action beyond its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred any federal or state lawsuit against firearm or ammunition manufacturers, distributors, dealers, importers, and their trade associations for harm caused when someone criminally or unlawfully misuses a gun. It would have also immediately dismissed every such lawsuit already in court on the day it became law, including suits brought by cities. Only two narrow exceptions were kept: suits against someone who knowingly handed a gun to be used in a violent or drug crime, and traditional negligence claims.
analysis.who_benefits: The firearm and ammunition industry, including manufacturers, distributors, dealers, importers, and their trade associations, would gain broad protection from civil lawsuits for harms caused by criminal misuse of their products. This included retroactive dismissal of pending suits brought by municipalities against the industry.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun makers, sellers, and trade associations

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibited any federal or state civil suit against gun or ammunition manufacturers, sellers, distributors, or importers for damages resulting from criminal or unlawful misuse of the product, and against industry trade associations as well [S2] [S3].

It went further than blocking future suits: any qualified civil liability action already pending on the date of enactment would have been dismissed immediately by the court hearing it, wiping out cases already filed, including municipal lawsuits [S3].

The bill kept only two exceptions: actions against a gun transferor convicted of a violent or drug-trafficking firearms offense, and actions against a seller for negligent entrustment or negligence per se [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Shooting victims and the municipalities suing on their behalf would bear the cost, losing the ability to hold gun sellers and manufacturers accountable in court for harm caused by criminal misuse — including suits already filed that would be thrown out. Taxpayers in those cities would forgo any recoveries the lawsuits might have produced.

drawbacks.text: Supporters argued the lawsuits targeted lawful, heavily regulated businesses for harm committed by criminals and third parties, and called the municipal suits an abuse of the legal system that threatened access to firearms for lawful purposes [S3].
An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill retroactively dismissed lawsuits already pending in court, cutting off claims that victims and cities had already filed [S3].

The exceptions were narrow: a victim could not sue a seller for negligent distribution unless the case fit negligent entrustment, negligence per se, or a transferor's criminal conviction — theories many negligence claims against high-volume sellers would not fit [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's protections would have extended well beyond shielding makers of nondefective guns from novel theories of liability: by barring nearly all suits arising from criminal misuse and throwing out pending cases, it would have closed the courthouse to victims and cities seeking to change how guns are marketed and distributed. The narrow exceptions would have left little room for ordinary negligence claims. Whatever the merits of limiting litigation against a regulated industry, the design leaned heavily toward the industry's interest.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and sat there with no hearing, no committee action, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Terry Everett introduced the Firearms Heritage Protection Act of 2003 in the House on January 27, 2003 [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
The bill attracted one cosponsor, a Democrat [S4].
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report, and no floor vote — before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Shooting victims and the municipalities that had sued gun sellers came out ahead, because their lawsuits survived and the industry remained exposed to civil liability for how its products reached criminals. The firearm industry did not get the legal shield it sought from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Victims and cities kept their day in court

for.name: Rep. Terry Everett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it was his only recorded action of consequence in its life.

against.name: F. James Sensenbrenner Jr.
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the committee — no hearing or markup in its two-year life, leaving it to die at referral.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no partisan split was recorded; the bill's only recorded support was its Republican sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor.

industries.industry: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, distributors, dealers, and importers
industries.note: The bill would have given the entire gun trade near-total immunity from civil suits over criminal misuse of its products, including throwing out lawsuits already filed by cities. Victims and municipalities would have lost their main legal lever for pressuring the industry on how guns reach the black market.

Trade associations of gun makers and sellers were explicitly covered, protecting them from suits as organizations — an unusual shield for industry groups. Their gain came directly at the cost of victims' and cities' legal claims.
